headline: Refuse a distrusted CA key wherever it appears, and trust only the platform store under useSystemStore.
summary: Eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates and their eight Sectigo cross-certificates were issued with P-384 private keys below 256, so anyone can forge a certificate under them. On Node 26.9.0, whose compiled-in roots still carry emSign ECC Root CA - G3, the toolkit accepted a forged chain wherever a caller opted into Node's roots or a host store: `tls.useSystemStore` on `pki.transport` and the ACME, EST, SCEP, CMP and CT clients, `pki fetch --system`, `pki.trust.systemAnchors({ allowNodeBundle: true })`, and a Windows store export passed to `systemAnchors`. This release adds a `distrustedKeys` option that refuses a CA key by the SHA-256 of its SubjectPublicKeyInfo on every path the toolkit validates and on every TLS connection it opens, narrows `useSystemStore` to the platform store, and adds a lint row that reports a key whose private scalar is that small. It also freezes the error-code surface and reads a `null` option the way an omitted one is read.

Security: `distrustedKeys` refuses a CA key by the SHA-256 of its DER SubjectPublicKeyInfo (64 hex characters or 32 bytes; `pki.trust.spkiDigest(cert)` computes one). `pki.path.validate` and `pki.path.build` fail a path that carries a listed key as the anchor, an intermediate or the target, with `path/distrusted-key`, and ask no revocation status at or below it. One entry covers every certificate for the key, so a cross-certificate under another root is refused too, including one that encodes the key another way: a compressed or hybrid EC point, explicit curve parameters, curve parameters inherited from the issuer, the id-ecDH or id-ecMQV identifier, RSA parameters without NULL, or an RSA key under the RSASSA-PSS or RSAES-OAEP identifier. A composite key is its own key, so listing one of its component keys does not list it. To refuse the eMudhra keys, list the eight SPKI digests published with the incident.

The verbs that validate a chain for the caller take the same option and apply it to every chain they build: `pki.cms.verify` (signer and timestamp chains), `pki.smime.verify`, `pki.tsp.verify`, `pki.cmp.verify`, `pki.cmp.openKeyPackage`, `pki.cmp.session` (response signer, issued certificate, key generation authority, root key update), `pki.possession.verifyRequest`, `pki.webauthn.verify` (pinned roots, metadata and SafetyNet roots), `pki.webauthn.verifyMetadataBlob` and `pki.sigstore.verifyBundle` (Fulcio and timestamp chains). `pki.ocsp.verify`, `pki.path.verifyOcspResponse`, `pki.path.ocspChecker` and `pki.path.fetchingChecker` do not accept an answer signed by a listed key, and a listed issuing CA authorizes no responder, its own or a delegate it certified. `pki.path.crlChecker` does not take a CRL whose issuer key is listed. A malformed list is the verb's own `<domain>/bad-input`, including on the verbs that otherwise report a chain failure as untrusted.

`tls.distrustedKeys` on `pki.transport.https` refuses a server whose verified chain carries a listed key, at any position including the root, with `transport/server-key-distrusted`, on the direct connection, `pki.transport.peerChain` and the origin inside a CONNECT tunnel. The transport checks the chain as a path of its own (each link signed by the certificate above it, each certificate in its validity period, each issuer a CA, the top a configured anchor's key), and it also follows every branch up through the configured anchors where an anchor that is not a root (an intermediate or cross-certificate, as the Windows platform store holds) issues a certificate on that chain. A server that sends another certificate with a listed intermediate's name, or a second path to a root the client does not trust, therefore cannot hide the chain the session was verified through. Node does not expose the chain OpenSSL verified, so while a list is set a session is refused when any chain it could have been verified through carries a listed key or fails these checks. An HTTPS proxy whose chain carries a key listed in `proxy.tls.distrustedKeys` or in the origin's list is refused with `transport/proxy-key-distrusted`. A request's list is added to the transport default's, which is read when the transport is built. The ACME, EST, SCEP, CMP and CT clients carry the list to every request, including a cross-origin redirect, under their own prefix (`acme/server-key-distrusted`, and so on).

A `tls` bag naming an option the transport does not read, such as a misspelled `distrustKeys`, is refused with `<domain>/bad-input` rather than ignored, on `pki.transport.https`, the ACME, EST, SCEP, CMP and CT clients, `pki.path.fetchingChecker` and the AIA fetch of `pki.path.build`. The `pki` command refuses a flag a verb does not take, and the `--name=value` form, so `pki verify ... --distrusted-keys <hex>` is a usage error rather than a verification with no list.

The `pki.est` verbs read `opts.tls` when they are called. They read it after an internal await, so a caller that changed the bag right after the call changed the policy the request was sent with. `pki.scep.enroll`, `getCert` and `getCrl` now carry a `tls` setting the bag inherits, as the other SCEP verbs already did, and `pki.est.fullcmc` carries a `tls` taken from a defaults object.

`tls.useSystemStore` trusts `tls.getCACertificates("system")` alone. It previously added Node's compiled-in roots, so a root that the host's CA package had removed was still trusted, and on Windows a chain that Node's own default verification rejected was accepted. When the platform store is empty, a request that names no `tls.anchors` is now refused with `transport/no-trust-anchors`; before, the empty list left the connection on Node's default store, which includes `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS`. The same applies to `proxy.tls`. `pki fetch --system` reads the platform store only.

`pki.trust.systemAnchors` returns only self-issued certificates as anchors. A certificate whose issuer name differs from its subject name, such as the Windows Intermediate Certification Authorities cache in a `certutil` export, is listed in `skipped` as `trust/not-self-issued` and returned in a new `intermediates` list for `pki.path.build` to use as candidates. It previously became an anchor that was never revocation-checked. `systemAnchors({ distrustedKeys })` leaves out a listed certificate, and `allowNodeBundle` now refuses a value that is not a boolean with `trust/bad-input` rather than reading it as off.

A `null` is refused where an omitted option means no restriction at all, because reading it as omitted dropped the check the caller asked for: `pki.path.validate` `requiredEku` and `checkPurpose`; `pki.webauthn.verify` `allowedAlgorithms`, `rootCertificates`, `metadata` and `tpmPolicy`; the metadata verb's `metadata`, `previousNo` and `statusPolicy`; `pki.trust` `purpose`; `pki.est` `expectedRecipientKeyId`; `pki.attrcert` `revocationStatus`; `pki.path.fetchingChecker` `allowPlaintextHttp`; and `pki.tls.decompressCertificate` `allowedAlgorithms`. A `null` `rootCertificates` or `metadata` on `pki.webauthn.verify` returned `attestationVerified: true` with `anchoredTo: null`. Each is now its module's `<domain>/bad-input`.

Every `expected*` and `require*` option on `pki.webauthn.verify`, and every member of a trust anchor, refuses a `null` rather than reading it as omitted. A `null` `expectedChallenge` would otherwise have verified the ceremony without the challenge comparison.
Added: `pki.trust.spkiDigest(cert)`: the SHA-256 of a certificate's DER SubjectPublicKeyInfo in canonical form (an uncompressed EC point with its named curve, RSA with NULL parameters) as lower-case hex, the entry `distrustedKeys` takes. For nearly every certificate this is the digest of the bytes it carries and the SPKI SHA-256 root programs publish. `cert` is DER, PEM or a parsed certificate.

`lint/key-compromise/small-ec-private-key` (CABF TLS BR 6.1.1.3 (4)) reports a P-256, P-384, P-521 or secp256k1 public key whose private scalar d, or n-d, is below 256. It runs in the default rule set for `pki.lint.certificate` and `pki.lint.csr` and under the new `key-compromise` profile, and it reports every one of the sixteen eMudhra certificates. The first check on each curve builds a table once per process (about 140 ms for P-384 and 320 ms for P-521 on Node 26).
Fixed: A request to a URL that names no port now sends `Host: name` rather than `Host: name:80` or `Host: name:443`. Some servers answer the port form with an error: emSign's CRL and OCSP endpoints returned HTTP 503, so `pki.path.fetchingChecker` could not determine the status of the revoked eMudhra intermediates, and with `softFail` it waived them.
An undetermined `pki.path.fetchingChecker` verdict names the OCSP failure and the CRL failure (`OCSP: ...; CRL: ...`). It previously kept only the CRL's reason.

`pki.transport.https` reads a `tls.anchors` Buffer that holds PEM text with a comment ahead of the armor as PEM. It previously read such a buffer as DER, and every connection under that anchor failed with `transport/server-auth-failed`.

A `null` option is read as the omitted option it stands for wherever an omitted option selects a documented default. `pki.est.serverkeygen` no longer refuses `requestedEncryption: null`, `pki.cms.compress` compresses at the default level for `level: null`, `pki.cms.digest` uses sha256 for `digestAlgorithm: null`, `pki.acme.downloadCertificate` no longer reports `boundToKey: true` for binding material given as `null`, `pki.path.validate` applies its documented limits for `maxPolicyNodes: null` and `minRsaModulusBits: null`, and `pki.x509.extension` accepts `critical: null` as non-critical.
Changed: `tls.useSystemStore` no longer includes Node's compiled-in roots. A caller that relied on them, for example in a container with no CA bundle installed, now gets `transport/no-trust-anchors`: install the host's CA bundle, or pass the roots you mean to trust as `tls.anchors` (`require("tls").rootCertificates` for Node's set).
`pki.trust.systemAnchors` no longer returns a certificate that is not self-issued as an anchor. Pass `result.intermediates` to `pki.path.build` as `candidates` to build a chain through them.

An unknown name in a `tls` bag, a `Proxy` as the `tls` bag of the ACME, EST, SCEP or CMP client, and an unknown flag or `--name=value` on the `pki` command are now refused. Spell the option as documented, pass a plain object, and give a flag's value as the next argument. A malformed `tls.distrustedKeys` in `pki.transport.https(defaults)` is refused when the transport is built.

The `domain/reason` error codes are a frozen contract, recorded in the api-snapshot and checked on every change: a code is not renamed or removed in a patch release. The seven ACME resource codes (`acme/bad-directory`, `acme/bad-order`, and the rest) are unchanged in value.
